claims.text: Suboptimal nutrition is a leading cause of poor health.
Evidence supports increased dietary consumption of fruits, nonstarchy vegetables, nuts, legumes, fish, vegetable oils, yogurt, and minimally processed whole grains for cardiometabolic health.
Evidence supports reduced dietary intake of red meats, processed meats, and foods rich in refined grains, starch, added sugars, salt, and trans fat for cardiometabolic health.
There is little evidence supporting the cardiometabolic relevance of popular food choices such as local, organic, grass-fed, farmed/wild, or non-genetically modified foods.
Personalized nutrition efficacy depends more on non-genetic characteristics than on genetic factors.

evidence.description: The authors state that suboptimal nutrition is a leading cause of poor health.
Evidence-informed dietary priorities include increased fruits, nonstarchy vegetables, nuts, legumes, fish, vegetable oils, yogurt, and minimally processed whole grains.
Evidence-informed dietary priorities include fewer red meats, processed meats, and foods rich in refined grains, starch, added sugars, salt, and trans fat.
Little evidence to date supports the cardiometabolic relevance of other popular priorities: eg, local, organic, grass-fed, farmed/wild, or non-genetically modified.
Evidence-based personalized nutrition appears to depend more on nongenetic characteristics (eg, physical activity, abdominal adiposity, gender, socioeconomic status, culture) than genetic factors.

methodologies.name: Narrative Literature and Policy Review
methodologies.description: A comprehensive review examining history, scientific evidence, controversies, and policy priorities related to diet, cardiovascular disease, obesity, and diabetes.

limitations.text: Evaluating dietary risk solely based on single isolated nutrients, blood lipids, or calorie counting rather than whole food patterns and diverse risk pathways is insufficient.

future_work.text: Further investigation is needed on the cardiometabolic effects of phenolics, dairy fat, probiotics, fermentation, coffee, tea, cocoa, eggs, specific vegetable and tropical oils, vitamin D, individual fatty acids, and diet-microbiome interactions.
